c.text: Chapter 2 – Leading Yourself First
The vineyard you forget to tend

There is a line in Song of Songs 1:6 that has followed me through twenty years of ministry. The young woman speaking says that they made her the keeper of the vineyards, but her own vineyard she has not kept.

In context she is talking about being sent out to work in the family’s fields under the sun while her own appearance suffered. But every leader I have ever met eventually reads that verse and goes quiet, because it describes exactly what happens to us. You are put in charge of other people’s spiritual growth, and somewhere in the middle of it you stop tending your own.

It happens faster than you would expect. Within a few months of leading, you notice that you have started reading the Bible only to find something to say. Your prayer life has become planning. You are producing spiritual food constantly and eating almost none of it.
That is the first thing this chapter is here to prevent.
Paul’s order of priority

1 Timothy 4:16 is one of the most direct instructions to a leader anywhere in Scripture. Paul, writing to Timothy in Ephesus, tells him to watch his life and his doctrine closely, and to persevere in them, because in doing so he will save both himself and his hearers.
Notice that Paul joins life and teaching together.
What Timothy teaches and how he lives both matter to the people he serves.
The point is not a ranking in which doctrine becomes secondary. Paul calls Timothy to persevere in both. A leader’s conduct can support the message or undermine it.
Jesus protected this, and he had more excuse than you

If anyone could have justified skipping personal prayer for the sake of urgent ministry, it was Jesus. The crowds were genuinely desperate. People were genuinely sick. The need was real and it never stopped.

Mark 1:35 sits right after an exhausting evening in Capernaum where the whole town gathered at the door and Jesus healed many. The next verse tells us that very early, while it was still dark, he got up, went out to a solitary place, and prayed. Simon and the others eventually came looking for him – the wording in verse 36 has a slight edge to it, as though they could not understand why he had disappeared when everyone wanted him.
Luke 5:16 makes clear that this was a repeated practice.

Jesus withdrew to quiet places and prayed even as crowds gathered to hear him and seek healing. The passage shows a rhythm of prayer amid demand; it does not give a formula linking busyness to hours of solitude. If the Son of God, in a three-year ministry, made time to be alone with the Father while people were literally waiting outside the door, then your ministry is not too urgent for it either.
The apostles refused a good job to protect this
Acts 6:1-4 is a story about a real administrative crisis.

The Greek-speaking widows in the Jerusalem church were being overlooked in the daily food distribution. This was not a trivial complaint – it was a genuine injustice with an ethnic dimension, in a church that was growing fast.

The Twelve’s response is striking. They say it would not be right for them to neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables, and they tell the church to choose seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and wisdom, to take responsibility for it. Then in verse 4 they state what they will give themselves to: prayer and the ministry of the word.
Notice what they did not do.

They did not dismiss the problem. They arranged for suitable people to address it while protecting their own responsibility for prayer and the ministry of the word. They shared the work instead of treating every need as theirs alone.

You will face a version of this within your first year. There will be a real need, and you will be the obvious person, and saying yes will quietly cost you the hours you were using to stay spiritually alive. Learning to say “this matters, and here is who should carry it” is a skill we will come back to in Chapter 5.
Integrity is what you are when it costs you nothing to be otherwise
The second half of leading yourself is integrity, and integrity is mostly a private matter.

Psalm 51 is David’s prayer after Nathan confronted him about Bathsheba and Uriah. What is worth noticing is where David locates the problem. In verse 6 he says God desires truth in the inward parts, and in verse 10 he asks God to create a clean heart in him and renew a right spirit within him. He does not ask for his reputation back. He asks for the inside to be dealt with.

The account in 2 Samuel 11 begins with David remaining in Jerusalem while his army is away. It then describes his abuse of power and his attempt to conceal it. The text does not tell us every private step that led there. It does show why repentance must address conduct and harm, not merely reputation.

The gap between private conduct and public responsibility is a danger for every leader. Proverbs 4:23 calls us to guard the heart because the course of our life flows from it. Attend to the source as well as what others can see.

Paul says something blunter in 1 Corinthians 9:27. Writing to a church in a city famous for its athletic games, he uses the image of a boxer and a runner, and says he disciplines his body and makes it his slave so that after preaching to others he himself will not be disqualified.
Paul thought it was possible to preach well and be disqualified personally. If he took that seriously, so should we.
What this looks like on a Tuesday
Theology is easy to agree with.
Here is the practical version.
Keep some Bible reading for your own growth.
Choose a book to read without the immediate pressure to turn it into a talk. Notice what you need to receive before deciding what you might teach.
Have a fixed time, not a hopeful intention.
“I’ll pray when I get a chance” reliably becomes no prayer. A modest fixed time you actually keep beats an ambitious one you abandon by February.
Find a trustworthy person who can ask honest questions.

A peer or experienced leader outside your direct team can help you reflect on your conduct, relationships and spiritual life. Agree what you will discuss and how confidentiality works. Meet monthly; honest accountability does not require surrendering passwords or all personal privacy.
Take a real day off, and let people see you take it.
Constant availability may reflect pressure, poor staffing or difficulty saying no. Whatever the cause, leaders need rest and a workable arrangement for urgent needs.
Notice strain before it becomes a crisis.

Tiredness, cynicism, isolation or small dishonesties deserve attention, though fatigue alone is not a moral failure. Ask what is happening and seek support rather than waiting for the situation to worsen.
You are the instrument here. Nobody else can maintain it for you.
